subsystems.name: Wide-field infrared telescope
subsystems.role: images a large patch of the Galactic bulge at once, in infrared so dust in the galactic plane does not hide the stars.

subsystems.name: Focal plane
subsystems.role: converts the crowded star field into digital images fast enough for short cadence.

subsystems.name: Observatory bus
subsystems.role: keeps the telescope thermally stable and pointed at the bulge for long stretches.

subsystems.name: Survey scheduling
subsystems.role: sets which fields are watched, how often, and in which filters.

subsystems.name: Event detection pipeline
subsystems.role: flags a brightening star within minutes so the event can be followed from the ground.

subsystems.name: Modelling and archive
subsystems.role: turns light curves into planet masses and separations.

buildSteps.title: Choose fields and cadence
buildSteps.detail: Designers pick bulge fields where stars are densest and set a repeat interval of roughly 15 minutes: short enough to catch planet signals that last only hours.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the optics
buildSteps.detail: A large lightweight mirror is ground, polished and coated, then mounted with a wide-field corrector that delivers a sharp image across a field of view of about a quarter of a square degree.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the focal plane
buildSteps.detail: Many near-infrared detector arrays — each a few thousand pixels on a side — are butted together into a mosaic of hundreds of megapixels, then tested for sensitivity and dark current.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and test the observatory
buildSteps.detail: Telescope, detectors, sunshade and spacecraft are assembled and shaken, heated and chilled in a thermal-vacuum chamber to prove they survive launch and space.

buildSteps.title: Launch, cool and commission
buildSteps.detail: After launch the detectors are cooled and the optics aligned, and the telescope takes calibration images before the survey begins.

buildSteps.title: Run the high-cadence survey
buildSteps.detail: The telescope stares at the bulge for months at a time, re-imaging the same fields thousands of times and subtracting each new frame from a reference image to find stars that have brightened.

buildSteps.title: Alert, then model
buildSteps.detail: Bright events trigger alerts so ground telescopes can observe the same star simultaneously; the combined space and ground light curve yields the planet-to-star mass ratio and, with parallax, the actual masses.

prerequisites.why: microlensing signals are faint, reddened and crowded; only big infrared arrays give the needed field and sensitivity.
a planet shows up as a bump lasting hours, so frames must be compared and measured continuously.
surveys that watch the bulge every clear night supply the event alerts and the simultaneous coverage needed for parallax.
measuring the same event from two widely separated viewpoints breaks the degeneracy that otherwise hides the lens mass.
millions of light curves must be searched and fitted; this is routine but data-hungry.

pathway.milestone: ground surveys watch the bulge nightly and find thousands of magnified stars a year, including dozens of planets and short events that hint at free-floating worlds
pathway.unlocks: a working alert network and a first statistical sample.

pathway.milestone: a dedicated space survey with a wide infrared field and rapid cadence, such as the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey planned for NASA's Roman Space Telescope, which is now being assembled and tested
pathway.unlocks: thousands of bound planets and a real census of worlds drifting free of any star.

pathway.milestone: planet demographics spanning masses from gas giants down to Mars-mass and separations from a fraction of an astronomical unit out to infinity
pathway.unlocks: tests of how planets form and get ejected, compared against the populations found by transits and radial velocity.

pathway.milestone: astrometric follow-up and joint analysis with other surveys to fix individual lens masses
pathway.unlocks: a three-dimensional picture of where planets sit in the galaxy.
